title: Family and Generations
description: Ten stories, letters and short reports about grandparents and grandchildren, family recipes and memories, family gatherings, raising children and caring for older parents.

lessons.title: The Apple Cake
lessons.summary: Lucy learns her grandmother's apple cake recipe and writes it down for the first time.
lessons.text:
Lucy is 16, and her grandmother, Rose, is 82. For more than 50 years, Rose has made the same apple cake for every family birthday. Everyone loves it. However, Rose has never written the recipe down. "It's all in my head," she always says.

Last month, Lucy decided that she wanted to learn the recipe properly. "If nobody learns it, one day the cake will be gone," she told her mother. So on Saturday morning, she took the bus to Rose's house.

When Lucy arrived, Rose had already put everything on the kitchen counter: flour, sugar, butter, eggs, milk and 4 green apples. The old blue bowl was waiting in the middle of the counter. Lucy recalled seeing that bowl on the same counter when she was a tiny child.

"How much flour do we need?" Lucy asked.
"Approximately 2 cups," Rose said.
"Approximately? I want to do this properly. I'm going to measure everything."
Rose laughed. "Fine. You measure, and I'll do the rest."

First, Rose cut the apples into tiny pieces. Then she mixed the butter and the sugar slowly with a wooden spoon. "Never do this fast," she said. "Slowly is the secret." Lucy measured each thing and wrote it down: 2 cups of flour, 1 cup of sugar, 3 eggs and half a cup of milk. Then Rose added the tiny pieces of apple and slowly mixed everything again.

The cake was in the oven for approximately an hour. Soon the whole house smelled of apples and butter. It was a familiar smell. Lucy recalled every birthday of her life, and she smiled. "This smell is so familiar," she said. "It smells like home."

When the cake was ready, Rose cut it into 12 equal portions. They each ate a portion with their tea, and Rose put the other portions in a box for Lucy's family.

"Thank you for teaching me," Lucy said. "I wish I had asked you years ago."
"It was a pleasure," Rose answered. "Cooking with you is the greatest pleasure I have."

That evening, Lucy's mother tasted the cake. "If you hadn't told me, I would have thought Rose made it," she said. Lucy was very proud. Next month, she will be making the cake for her brother's birthday, all by herself.

Questions:
Why did Lucy want to learn the recipe?
She wanted to learn it because Rose had never written it down.
What was on the kitchen counter?
Flour, sugar, butter, eggs, milk and 4 green apples were on the counter.
Why did Lucy want to measure everything?
She wanted to learn the recipe properly.
What is Rose's secret?
Her secret is to mix the butter and the sugar slowly.
What did Lucy recall when she smelled the cake?
She recalled every birthday of her life, because the smell was so familiar.
How many portions did Rose cut?
She cut the cake into 12 equal portions.

lessons.title: The Big Family Weekend
lessons.summary: Carol writes to her whole family to invite them to a weekend for her parents' 60th wedding anniversary.
lessons.text:
Subject: Mom and Dad's 60th anniversary

Dear family,

As most of you know, June 14 will be Mom and Dad's 60th wedding anniversary. By then, they will have been married for 60 years! To celebrate this special occasion, my brother Tom and I have organized a weekend for the whole extended family. This is the first time that we have organized something so big, so please read this email to the end.

The weekend will be at Pine Lake Park, where Mom and Dad met in 1965. We are expecting approximately 80 people. Our extended family has grown a lot in the last few years, and many of the children have never met each other. For this reason, everyone will wear a name tag. When you arrive, please take a tag, write your name on it, and also write whose son, daughter or grandchild you are. I know name tags sound a little silly, but they will really help.

As always, we will follow our old family custom: the big family photo at noon on Saturday. Dad started this custom in 1980, and we have a photo from every family weekend since then. Please don't be late for the photo!

On Saturday afternoon, there will be a card tournament. The card tournament is another custom. Dad has won it 11 times, and he says he will be winning it again this year. Besides the tournament, there will be games for the children and a swim in the lake. In the evening, Mom will be telling the story of how she met Dad. We have all heard it many times, but it's still a nice story.

I know that not everyone can afford a hotel for 2 nights. If you can't afford it, please tell me. Some of us live near the park and have extra rooms. We will be happy to have a visitor or two. Last time, my house had 6 visitors, and it was a lot of fun.

Finally, please don't buy expensive presents. Mom and Dad say that the best present on this occasion is having all of us together.

I'm looking forward to seeing you all.

Love,
Carol

Questions:
What occasion is the family celebrating?
They are celebrating Mom and Dad's 60th wedding anniversary.
Why is the weekend at Pine Lake Park?
It is there because Mom and Dad met at the park in 1965.
What should everyone write on their name tag?
They should write their name and whose son, daughter or grandchild they are.
What is the family custom at noon on Saturday?
The custom is the big family photo.
What will there be besides the card tournament?
Besides the tournament, there will be games for the children and a swim in the lake.
What can people do if they can't afford a hotel?
They can tell Carol, and they can stay with family members who live near the park.

lessons.title: The Loud Guitar
lessons.summary: Max's loud guitar bothers his family until his grandfather finds a calm solution.
lessons.text:
My name is Anna, and I have two sons, Ben and Max. They are brothers, but they have opposite personalities. Ben is 16. He is quiet and calm, and he loves reading. Max is 14, and he is the opposite: he is loud, he talks all the time, and he can't sit still. My father, Walter, lives with us. He says Max has the same personality that he had at that age.

For his birthday, Max got a guitar. He was so happy that he played it in his bedroom every evening for 3 hours. The problem was that he played it very loud. The noise filled the whole house. It bothered Ben, who was trying to study in the next bedroom. It bothered me while I was working. It even bothered the dog, who hid under the table every time Max started to play.

At first, I tried to stay calm. "Max, please play a little more quietly," I said. But the next evening, the noise was just as loud as before. After a week, I couldn't stay calm anymore. "If this noise doesn't stop, you will have to quit the guitar," I told him. Max was very upset. "I'm not going to quit!" he said, and he closed his bedroom door.

That night, my father came into the kitchen. "Ah, Anna," he said. "Don't make him quit. When I was 14, I had a guitar too, and I was just as loud. My mother wanted me to quit, but my father taught me to play properly. Let me talk to Max."

The next day, Walter took his old guitar out of a box and knocked on Max's bedroom door. I don't know exactly what he said. But after that, everything changed. Walter taught Max that a good player doesn't need to be loud. He showed him how to play slowly and softly. They moved the practice from the bedroom to the garage, where the noise doesn't bother anyone.

Now they play together every evening, and the house is calm again. Ben can study, and the dog has come out from under the table. Last week, Max said to me, "Ah, Mom, I'm glad I didn't quit." I'm glad too. If my father hadn't helped, Max would have quit the guitar. I should have talked to Walter much earlier.

Questions:
How are Ben's and Max's personalities different?
They have opposite personalities: Ben is quiet and calm, and Max is loud.
Who did the noise bother?
It bothered Ben, Anna and even the dog.
What did Anna tell Max after a week?
She told him that if the noise didn't stop, he would have to quit the guitar.
How did Walter help?
He taught Max to play slowly and softly, and they moved the practice to the garage.
What would have happened if Walter hadn't helped?
Max would have quit the guitar.

lessons.title: Dad Walks Again
lessons.summary: After a fall, Frank's daughter helps him get stronger and live at home again.
lessons.text:
Monday, March 3

Last week, my father, Frank, fell in his garden and broke his hip. He is 79 and lives alone, so this was a big problem for him and for me, his only daughter. The fall has affected every part of his life. He can't walk to the store, he can't drive, and he can't even take a shower by himself.

Today I talked to his doctor, Dr. Hill. "Under the circumstances, he shouldn't live alone for a while," she said. "And I can't permit him to drive for at least 3 months." So, for now, Dad is staying with me and my family.

Tuesday, March 11

Dad is very determined. "I'm going to walk to my own mailbox again," he says every morning. A nurse comes to my house 3 times a week. She has shown Dad some exercises to make the muscles in his legs stronger. He also has to stretch every morning and every evening. At first, he could only stretch for a few minutes, but now he can stretch for 20 minutes. He is so determined that he sometimes does more exercises than the nurse asks.

The nurse also talked about his diet. Dad has always loved salt and cheese. "For strong muscles and bones, you need a better diet," she said. "More fish, more vegetables and more milk." Dad was not happy about the new diet, but he agreed to try it.

Saturday, April 5

We have made Dad's own house ready for him. We put a seat in the shower and a rail next to it, so he can take a shower safely. Because he can't drive, we have organized a food delivery. Every Friday, a delivery comes from the store with milk, fish, fruit and vegetables for his new diet. The delivery driver even carries the bags into the kitchen.

Monday, June 2

Today Dad moved back home. I was a little worried about him living alone again. But the circumstances are different now: he is much stronger, and his house is safe. Holding the rail, he walked down the steps. Then he walked slowly to his mailbox and back. He smiled at me and said, "I told you I would do it."

Dr. Hill will check his hip again next month. If everything is fine, she will permit him to drive again. I must say, I have never seen anyone so determined.

Questions:
How has the fall affected Frank's life?
He can't walk to the store, he can't drive, and he can't take a shower by himself.
Why can't Frank drive?
The doctor can't permit him to drive for at least 3 months.
What did the nurse show him?
She showed him exercises to make the muscles in his legs stronger.
What is in his new diet?
His new diet has more fish, more vegetables and more milk.
What comes every Friday?
A food delivery comes from the store every Friday.
Why is Frank staying with his daughter for now?
The doctor said that, under the circumstances, he shouldn't live alone for a while.

lessons.title: A Day on the Boat
lessons.summary: Leo goes out on the Pacific with his grandfather, who tells him about his life at sea.
lessons.text:
Leo is 11 years old. Every summer, he visits his grandfather, Harold, who lives in a small town on the Pacific coast. Harold was a fisherman for 40 years. He has a small boat, and he knows every rock and every wave in that part of the Pacific.

This summer, Harold said, "Tomorrow we're going out on the boat. It's going to be a real adventure."

They left at 6 in the morning. The air on the Pacific was cold, so they both wore a warm coat. "Hold on tight," Harold said when the boat started to move. Leo held on tight with both hands, and his heart was beating fast.

While they were fishing, Harold told Leo about his life at sea. "I've had a lot of adventures," he said. "Once, I had an encounter with a whale. It came up right next to my boat. It was incredible. It was longer than my house!" Leo's eyes grew wide. "That's incredible," he said. "Were you afraid?" "A little," Harold answered. "But the whale was calm, and so was I."

Then Harold put a small piece of fish on Leo's hook and showed him how to throw the line. After 20 minutes, Leo felt something pull. "Hold the line tight!" Harold said. Leo pulled slowly, and soon a big silver fish came out of the water. It was hanging from his hook. Leo was so proud.

On the way home, they saw a group of seals on the rocks. One seal swam close to the boat. "That seal must be hungry," Harold laughed. "Seals love fish. Years ago, a seal stole a fish right off my hook. That was a funny encounter."

Harold also told Leo about marine life. "The Pacific is full of life: fish, seals, whales and many other marine animals. Some scientists spend their whole lives studying marine life."

"I want to do that," Leo said. "I want to be a marine scientist."

That evening, Leo called his mother. "Today was the greatest adventure of my life," he said. "If I hadn't come here this summer, I would never have seen the seals." Harold smiled and put his old coat on Leo's shoulders. "You can keep it," he said. "You will need a good coat for your next adventure."

Questions:
Where does Harold live?
He lives in a small town on the Pacific coast.
Why did they wear a warm coat?
They wore a warm coat because the air on the Pacific was cold.
What incredible encounter did Harold tell Leo about?
He told Leo about an encounter with a whale that came up next to his boat.
What did Leo catch?
He caught a big silver fish on his hook.
What did they see on the rocks?
They saw a group of seals on the rocks.
What does Leo want to be?
He wants to be a marine scientist.

lessons.title: A Full House Again
lessons.summary: When their children leave home, Paul and Linda adopt a dog and enjoy a weekend with their grandson.
lessons.text:
Paul and Linda have 3 children, but all of them have grown up and moved to other cities. After the youngest one left, the house felt empty. Her bedroom was empty, the kitchen was quiet, and nobody played music anymore. "This house is too empty," Linda said one evening. "Let's get a pet."

The next Saturday, they went to an animal rescue center. A rescue center takes care of dogs and cats that have no home. They saw a lot of dogs, but one small brown dog came straight to Paul and put its nose in his coat pocket. "He must smell the cookies in my pocket," Paul laughed. They took the dog home and called him Lucky. Since then, Paul always keeps a few dog treats in his pocket, and Lucky follows him everywhere. The rescue dog has become the perfect pet.

Last month, their grandson, Jack, came to stay for a weekend. Jack is 15, and he has grown very tall. He is now taller than Paul. "You're so tall!" Linda said when he arrived. Jack plays basketball, and his team was in the playoffs. On Saturday, Paul and Linda went to his playoff game. They cheered for him the whole time. Jack's team won the playoff game by 6 points.

That evening, Paul took a box of old comic books out of the closet. He had kept them since he was a child. Jack had only read comics on his phone before. He had never held a real comic book. He sat on the sofa with Lucky and read comic after comic until midnight.

On Sunday morning, Linda made the usual family breakfast: eggs, toast and pancakes. When the children were young, she had made this breakfast every Sunday. "This is the usual Sunday breakfast?" Jack asked. "It's incredible! At home, we usually just have cereal." After breakfast, they took Lucky for a long walk in the park.

When Jack left, he put a small note in Paul's pocket. It said, "Thank you for the comics and the breakfast. Can I come again for the next playoff game?" Paul read the note and smiled. The house didn't feel so empty anymore.

Questions:
Why did the house feel empty?
It felt empty because all of the children had grown up and moved away.
What does a rescue center do?
It takes care of dogs and cats that have no home.
Why did the dog put its nose in Paul's pocket?
It must have smelled the cookies in Paul's pocket.
How tall is Jack now?
He is taller than Paul.
What did Linda make on Sunday morning?
She made the usual family breakfast: eggs, toast and pancakes.
What did Jack read until midnight?
He read Paul's old comic books.

lessons.title: Helen Joins Twitter
lessons.summary: Helen, a retired journalist, learns to tweet with the help of her granddaughter.
lessons.text:
Helen is 76. For 40 years, she worked as a journalist for a city newspaper. For the last 15 of those years, she was the newspaper's food critic. Every week, she ate at a different restaurant and wrote about it. People said she was the best critic in the city.

Now Helen is retired, and she misses writing. One day, her granddaughter, Maya, said, "You should start using Twitter. You can tweet about food and restaurants, just like in your newspaper."

"But I don't know anything about tweets," Helen said. "The newspaper was my medium. I don't understand this new medium."

"I'll teach you," Maya said.

First, they had a problem: Helen's old house had no internet. Phone coverage was also bad in her part of town, so she couldn't use the internet on her phone. "With this coverage, your phone is not enough," Maya said. "You need a cable." So Maya called a company, and a man came and put a new cable through the wall. The cable went from the street to Helen's living room. After that, the internet was fast.

Then Maya showed Helen how to write a tweet. "A tweet has to be short," she explained. "And it has to be relevant. People don't want to read about everything. They want relevant information: where to eat, what to order and how much it costs."

Helen wrote her first tweet. It was much too long. "Now you have to edit it," Maya said. Helen laughed. "Edit? I was a journalist for 40 years. I know how to edit!" She started editing. She made the tweet short and clear, and then she read it again and made one more small edit. Finally, she tweeted: "Lunch at the new Greek restaurant on Main Street. Excellent fish soup, $9. Go early, because it gets busy."

By the next morning, 200 people had read it. A week later, a local journalist wrote an article about her. The title was "The Food Critic Is Back."

Now Helen tweets every day. She is still a critic, but she has found a new medium. "If you hadn't helped me, I would never have tried it," she told Maya. "I wish I had started years ago."

Questions:
What was Helen's job?
She was a journalist and the newspaper's food critic.
Why didn't the internet work in her house at first?
Her house had no internet, and the phone coverage was bad.
What did the man put through the wall?
He put a new cable through the wall.
What does a tweet have to be?
A tweet has to be short and relevant.
Why did Helen laugh when Maya said "edit"?
She laughed because she had been a journalist for 40 years and knew how to edit.

lessons.title: After the Flood
lessons.summary: A farm family and their neighbors work together after a flood.
lessons.text:
George is a farmer. He is 72, and he has lived on the same farm by the river all his life. His father was a farmer, and his grandfather was a farmer too. Now George runs the farm with his son, Mike.

Last April, it started to rain, and it didn't stop for days. The river rose higher and higher. On the 8th day, the radio said there would be a flood. "We have to move the cows," George said. That evening, George and Mike walked the cows up the old trail behind the barn. The trail goes up a hill, where the ground is high and dry. It was dark and wet, and the trail was full of mud, but they got all 40 cows to the top.

That night, the flood came. In the morning, the farm looked like a lake. Mike measured the depth of the water in the barn. It was approximately 3 feet. Unfortunately, the water had also reached the house. The family had to go up to the second floor, and they watched the rain hit the roof. Mike's wife, Sarah, and their two children were with them. "Let's pray," George's wife, Mary, said. The family belongs to the small Catholic church in town, and they pray together every Sunday. That morning, they prayed for the rain to stop.

On the 10th day, the rain finally stopped, and the sun came out. "It feels like heaven," Mary said. Slowly, the water went down. Every day, Mike measured its depth again.

Unfortunately, the flood had destroyed most of the corn. The water had also damaged the roof of the barn. But nobody was hurt, and all the cows were safe on the hill. "Thank heaven we moved them," George said. "If we hadn't taken them up the trail, we would have lost them all."

The next Saturday, people from the Catholic church came to help. Other farmers came too. They cleaned the house, and they repaired the roof of the barn. Mike's son, who is 12, carried water and sandwiches to everyone. By evening, the roof was as good as new.

"I've been a farmer for 50 years," George said that night. "I've seen 3 floods. But I've never seen so many people help."

Questions:
Why did George and Mike move the cows?
They moved them because the radio said there would be a flood.
Where does the trail go?
It goes up a hill behind the barn, where the ground is high and dry.
What was the depth of the water in the barn?
It was approximately 3 feet.
Why did the family pray?
They prayed for the rain to stop.
What would have happened if they hadn't moved the cows?
They would have lost all the cows.
Who came to help the next Saturday?
People from the Catholic church and other farmers came to help.

lessons.title: Thirty Years on the Town Council
lessons.summary: A short newspaper report about Ruth Miller, who is leaving the town council, and her granddaughter.
lessons.text:
After 30 years on the town council, Ruth Miller, 78, attended her last meeting on Tuesday evening. More than 100 people came to the council chamber to thank her. The chamber was so full that some people had to stand outside the door.

Ms. Miller was first elected to the council in 1995. Before that, she was a teacher at the high school. "I wanted to make our town better for children and for older people," she said. Since then, she has been elected 7 times. Voters have always supported her, because she listens to them. "Every voter is important," she said. "When a voter calls me, I always call back."

From 2010 to 2018, Ms. Miller was the town's deputy mayor. As deputy mayor, she worked closely with the mayor, Tom Grant. "Ruth was my best ally," Mr. Grant said on Tuesday. "When I needed help, she was always there. She was an ally to everyone who wanted to make this town better."

During her 30 years, the council approved many of her ideas. In 2001, it approved her plan for a new library. Later, it approved a free bus for older people. Not every idea was approved, of course. In 2005, the council rejected her plan for a new park. "They rejected it, but I didn't give up," she said. She brought the plan back 2 years later, and this time nobody rejected it. The town worked hard to implement the plan, and the park opened in 2008. "It's one thing to have a good idea," she said. "It's another thing to implement it."

At the end of the meeting, the council voted on one last motion. The motion was to give the new park her name. Everyone in the chamber voted yes, and the motion passed.

One person in the chamber was especially proud: Ms. Miller's granddaughter, Emma, 24. Emma said her grandmother had inspired her. "When I was a child, she took me to council meetings. She inspired me to help other people." Next year, Emma will be running for the town council herself.

"If Emma is elected, I'll be her first ally," Ms. Miller said with a smile.

Questions:
When was Ruth Miller first elected to the council?
She was first elected in 1995.
Why have voters always supported her?
They have supported her because she listens to them.
What was her job from 2010 to 2018?
She was the town's deputy mayor, and the mayor said she was his best ally.
What happened to her plan for a new park in 2005?
The council rejected it, but she brought it back 2 years later.
What was the last motion of the meeting?
The motion was to give the new park her name.
Who was inspired by Ruth Miller?
Her granddaughter, Emma, was inspired by her.

lessons.title: Young People Today
lessons.summary: In a short column, a grandfather explains why he no longer complains about young people's manners.
lessons.text:
Whenever I meet people my age, the conversation soon turns to young people. My friends complain that teenagers are always on their phones. They complain that young people have no manners. "When we were young," they say, "we said please and thank you, and we respected older people." I have to admit that I was guilty of this too. For years, I complained about young people whenever I had the chance.

Then, last year, my wife and I spent a month with our son's family, and I changed my mind. My grandchildren are 13 and 17. At first, it seemed obvious to me that they spent too much time on their phones. But when I watched more closely, I saw what they were doing. My granddaughter was using her phone to study Spanish. My grandson was using his to help his friend with math. Neither of them was wasting time.

Their manners surprised me too. When I came into the room, they said hello. When I needed help with my new phone, they helped me, and they never laughed at me. At dinner, they asked me questions about my life and listened to the answers. Their manner was polite and kind. Basically, they were just like we were at their age, only with phones.

So I began to think that our idea about young people is false. Let me try to be objective. It is true that young people today use phones a lot. But it is false that they have no manners. It is also false that they don't care about older people. To be objective, every generation complains about the next one. My grandfather complained about my manners, and I'm sure my grandchildren will be complaining about their grandchildren in 50 years.

I feel a little guilty now. I wish I had spent more time with young people instead of complaining about them. If I had listened to them earlier, I would have learned a lot.

The answer seems obvious to me now. Basically, if we want young people to respect us, we should respect them first. Whenever my friends complain, I now tell them about my grandchildren. Some of them still don't believe me. But a few of them have started to listen.

Questions:
What do the writer's friends complain about?
They complain that teenagers are always on their phones and have no manners.
Why did the writer feel guilty?
He felt guilty because for years he had complained about young people too.
What was his granddaughter doing on her phone?
She was using it to study Spanish.
How were the grandchildren's manners?
Their manners were polite and kind.
Is it true that young people have no manners?
No. The writer thinks that this idea is false.
What does the writer think we should do?
He thinks that if we want young people to respect us, we should respect them first.
